title: Parametric Quantum Feature Selection Methods for Fraud and Default Detection
abstract_summary: The paper formulates feature selection as a QUBO problem and introduces three new parametric QUBO formulations (parametric-MI, MI-Pearson, and parametric distance correlation) solved using quantum annealing (hybrid solvers). Extensive experiments on multiple credit card fraud and default datasets show QUBO-based feature selection on quantum annealers consistently outperforms classical feature selection baselines, with parametric-MI offering a practical trade-off between performance and computational cost.
methodology_description: The authors formulate feature selection as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem and solve it using quantum annealing (via a hybrid quantum-classical solver). They propose three new QUBO constructions (parametric-MI, MI-Pearson, and parametric Distance Correlation) in addition to existing QUBO formulations from the literature (Pearson-correlation QUBO, SVC-Boost QUBO, and MIQUBO). For each QUBO construction they build a Q-matrix whose diagonal terms encourage relevance to the target and off-diagonal terms penalize redundancy; when desired they add a penalization term (sum_i x_i - k)^2 to fix the number of selected features. The workflow: preprocess datasets (remove non-numeric features, zero-variance features, and all-NaN features), compute pairwise metrics needed for Q (Pearson r, mutual information, conditional mutual information for MIQUBO, or distance correlation), form QUBO matrices (with tunable scaling parameter alpha for parametric formulations), solve the QUBO using a D-Wave hybrid solver (and also compare with simulated annealing), obtain the binary selection vector, train an XGBoost classifier on the selected features, and evaluate model performance using F1 score and Gini (AUC-related) on held-out test data. They compare quantum-selected feature sets against classical feature-selection baselines (Random Forest feature importance; mutual information + Spearman correlation) and against models trained on the full feature sets. Experiments sweep number of selected features k and, where applicable, the alpha scaling parameter to assess sensitivity and performance trade-offs.
algorithms_used: Support Vector Classifier (used in SVC-Boost QUBO formulation)
experimental_setup: QUBO problems (constructed from dataset-specific pairwise statistics) were solved primarily with a hybrid quantum-classical annealing solver (D-Wave hybrid solver that decomposes large QUBOs to fit QPU connectivity). Because current QPUs have limited connectivity, the hybrid solver was used. For comparison, a classical simulated annealer was also used to solve the same QUBOs. Selected features were used to train XGBoost classifiers; evaluation was performed on held-out test sets (80/20 split for two datasets; provided train/test files for the default dataset).
dataset_used: Three public Kaggle financial datasets: (1) Credit Card Fraud (ULB 2017) — ~300K transactions, 30 features; (2) Large credit-card fraud (Vesta/IEEE-CIS dataset, Howard et al. 2019) — originally 433 features and 144K samples, after preprocessing 280 features; (3) American Express Default Prediction (Howard et al. 2022) — monthly-12 data, originally 182 features, after preprocessing 174 features. Targets are binary (fraud / default).

sources: Kaggle - ULB credit card fraud dataset (2017) - https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud/data
experiment_input.preprocessing: Removed non-numeric features, features with zero variance, and features with all NaN values. For the first two datasets an 80/20 train/test split was used. For the Amex default dataset the provided monthlytrain-12 and monthlytest-12 files were used.
experiment_input.notes: Pairwise statistics (Pearson correlation, mutual information, conditional mutual information for MIQUBO, distance correlation) are computed from training data to build Q matrices.

steps: Preprocess dataset (drop non-numeric, zero variance, all-NaN features).
Compute pairwise feature-feature and feature-target metrics required for each QUBO variant (Pearson r, mutual information (MI), conditional mutual information (CMI) for MIQUBO, distance correlation).
- Pearson QUBO: Q_ij = r(fi,fj) for i≠j, Q_ii = -r(fi,y).
- SVC-Boost QUBO: train single-feature SVCs to get predictions hi and compute correlations (per cited formulation).
- Parametric-MI: Q_ij = (1-α) * MI(fi,fj) for i≠j; Q_ii = -α * MI(fi,y).
- MI-Pearson: Q_ij = α * r(fi,fj) for i≠j; Q_ii = -MI(fi,y).
- Parametric Distance Correlation: Q_ij = DC(fi,fj) for i≠j; Q_ii = -α * DC(fi,y).
Optionally add penalty term (Σ_i x_i - k)^2 to enforce selecting exactly k features.
Sweep k (number of selected features) across ranges appropriate for dataset (examples: 13, 25 for small dataset; 25 to 200 step 25 for large dataset; 25 to 150 step 25 for default dataset).
For parametric formulations sweep or tune α in [0,1] (parametric-MI examined α sensitivity; MI-Pearson experiments used α=1).
Solve each QUBO instance using D-Wave hybrid solver (and for comparison via simulated annealing).
Take resulting binary selection vector, train XGBoost classifier on training data restricted to selected features, evaluate on test data.
Record F1 and Gini metrics and compare across methods and to baseline (full-feature model).

key_findings: [supported] QUBO-based feature selection (using quantum annealing/hybrid solvers) yields comparable or improved ML performance (F1 and Gini) relative to several classical feature-selection baselines across three real-world credit-card datasets.

[supported] The newly proposed parametric-MI QUBO formulation achieves performance comparable to MIQUBO while being less computationally expensive (favorable trade-off between performance and complexity).

[supported] The MI-Pearson QUBO formulation is particularly effective for datasets containing both linear and non-linear feature–feature / feature–target relationships (example: small ULB fraud dataset), and achieved the highest Gini reported in that experiment.
[supported] MIQUBO better captures higher-order feature interactions and performs best when such interactions are present (example: large fraud and default datasets in the paper).
[supported] Introducing a tunable scaling parameter (alpha) in parametric formulations helps tune feature selection quality, especially when the allowed number of selected features is small.
[supported] In the authors' experiments, training the downstream ML model (XGBoost) on quantum-selected feature subsets often matched or outperformed models trained on the full feature set.
[supported] Feature subsets produced by hybrid quantum annealing and by simulated annealing showed similar ML performance in the reported experiments.

[supported] Practical use required a hybrid solver (classical + quantum annealer) because current QPUs cannot directly handle large, densely connected QUBOs; the hybrid decomposition approach was used for the experiments.

[speculative] Mapping feature selection to QUBO and solving with quantum annealing provides a path toward better scalability for some combinatorial FS instances (theoretical promise emphasized in introduction and citations).

[speculative] Statements that quantum annealers are generally less affected by noise and can handle significantly larger system sizes than gate-based quantum computers are presented as background motivation (not directly proven by the paper's experiments).
[speculative] The NP-hardness of exact feature subset selection is referenced as theoretical motivation for exploring quantum-computing-based optimization approaches.
results_summary: The paper formulates feature selection as QUBO problems and introduces three new parameterized QUBO constructions (parametric-MI, MI-Pearson, parametric distance correlation). Using a hybrid quantum annealing workflow, the authors benchmark these against established QUBO methods (Pearson, SVC-Boost, MIQUBO) and classical baselines (Random Forest importance; mutual information + Spearman). Across three credit-card datasets (small ULB fraud, larger Vesta fraud, and an AmEx default dataset) they find that quantum-selected subsets often match or slightly exceed classical baselines and sometimes even outperform models trained on the full feature set. Parametric-MI provides a good performance/complexity trade-off vs MIQUBO; MI-Pearson is strong when linear + nonlinear relations coexist; MIQUBO is advantageous when higher-order interactions dominate. The authors also report that simulated annealing produces similar FS performance to hybrid quantum annealing in their experiments.
performance_claims: Small fraud dataset (ULB 2017, ~30 features, ~300K samples): best reported F1 = 0.87356 (MI-Spearman, k=25); best reported Gini = 97.67777% (MI-Pearson, k=13).
Large fraud dataset (original 433 features → 280 after preprocessing, 144K samples): best reported F1 = 0.77935 (Parametric-MI, k=204); best reported Gini = 92.71444% (MI-Pearson, k=198).
Credit default dataset (182 features → 174 after preprocessing): best reported F1 = 0.68827 (MIQUBO, k=150); best reported Gini = 85.07098% (MIQUBO, k=150).
Parametric tuning (alpha) strongly influences F1 and Gini when selecting small k (number of features); influence diminishes as k increases (visualized in paper's plots).

Hybrid quantum annealing vs simulated annealing: selected-feature models produced near-identical ML metrics in the authors' experiments (example plot shows F1 ~0.67 and Gini ~84–85 for parametric-MI across QA and SA).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors report empirical improvements in selected cases and argue quantum annealing (via hybrid solvers) is a promising approach for combinatorial FS; however the experimental results are dataset-dependent, sometimes matched or closely replicated by classical simulated annealing, and do not demonstrate a clear, unambiguous quantum computational advantage across all tested settings.
limitations: MIQUBO is computationally expensive: computing higher-order conditional mutual information (CMI) increases time and memory requirements with sample size (author-stated).

Current quantum annealers (QPU) have limited qubit connectivity and are not suitable for large or densely connected QUBO; the authors had to use hybrid solvers that decompose problems (author-stated).

Quantum annealers operate with finite annealing times, environmental noise, and decoherence; these factors can suppress coherent tunneling and make QA dynamics resemble classical thermal hopping, reducing potential QA advantage (author-stated).
Performance is dataset-dependent: different QUBO formulations perform better for different datasets and feature-interaction structures (author-stated).
Parametric models require careful tuning (e.g., choice of α) — particularly important when selecting a small number of features (author-stated).
[inferred] Experiments are limited to three Kaggle credit-card datasets; generalizability to other financial products, data regimes, or real-world production systems is not demonstrated.
[inferred] Categorical / non-numeric features were removed prior to QUBO construction, indicating a limitation in handling mixed data types in the presented pipeline.
[inferred] Use of hybrid decomposition (classical + quantum) may affect solution quality and makes it hard to isolate pure quantum advantage.
[inferred] Observed improvements over classical baselines are sometimes small; practical economic benefit is asserted but not quantified.
[inferred] The paper does not evaluate robustness of selected features over time (dataset drift) or under adversarial conditions common in fraud detection.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — QUBO-based feature selection solved via a D-Wave hybrid annealer consistently outperforms classical feature-selection baselines (Random Forest importance, MI+Spearman) on multiple large public fraud and default datasets according to F1 and Gini metrics.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Practical workflow uses classical preprocessing (pairwise statistics: Pearson, MI, CMI, distance correlation) to build QUBO matrices and a D-Wave hybrid solver to decompose/solve large QUBOs, followed by classical XGBoost classification on selected features.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Introduces three parametric QUBO formulations (parametric-MI, MI-Pearson, parametric distance correlation); parametric-MI provides a tunable trade-off between relevance and redundancy and is presented as practically useful on current hybrid annealing platforms.

#limitation:qubit-count — Authors explicitly rely on D-Wave hybrid decomposition due to limited QPU connectivity/capacity; scalability to pure QPU runs or much larger feature spaces without hybridization is not demonstrated.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Empirical evaluation covers three real-world Kaggle datasets of varying feature dimensionality (30, ~280, ~174 post-preproc) with sweeps over k (selected features) and alpha (where applicable), demonstrating robustness of QUBO formulations across datasets and selection sizes.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical simulated annealing is used as a baseline QUBO solver in comparisons, indicating the experimental design benchmarks hybrid quantum-assisted annealing against classical heuristics.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Paper reports quantitative results (F1, Gini) on held-out test sets but omits low-level solver and model hyperparameters (annealing reads/times, XGBoost hyperparameters, random seeds, number of solver runs), limiting reproducibility and detailed performance attribution.
